title: Amos
summary: Amos is a biblical book focused on justice, judgment, worship integrity, covenant accountability, and restoration.
historical_context: Amos confronts injustice and empty worship while holding out restoration beyond judgment.
ancient_near_east_context: Amos belongs to the ancient Mediterranean and Near Eastern world reflected in its setting, institutions, and canonical placement.
hebraic_worldview: Amos should be read with attention to covenant memory, communal identity, worship, wisdom, and accountability before the Lord.
second_temple_context: Second Temple readers received Amos as part of Israel's Scriptures and read it within questions of identity, worship, exile, and hope.
canonical_context: Within Minor Prophets, book 3 of 12, Amos contributes to the Bible's unfolding witness by connecting justice, judgment, worship integrity, covenant accountability, and restoration to the larger storyline.
later_christian_reception: Christian interpretation has read Amos as part of the canonical witness to faithfulness, judgment, mercy, and hope in Christ-centered Scripture reading.
literary_context: Amos uses prophecy, poetry within Minor Prophets, book 3 of 12 to develop its themes through the book's structure and key passages.
covenantal_significance: Amos helps readers trace covenant faithfulness, failure, mercy, and hope within its canonical setting.
authorship_positions: Traditional prophetic attribution to the named prophet
Many scholars recognize collection and editorial shaping
date_ranges: 8th-5th centuries BCE, depending on the prophet
Final forms often reflect later collection and editing
original_audience: Israel and Judah under covenant accountability before and after exile
historical_setting: Assyrian, Babylonian, and post-exilic settings across the prophetic corpus
canonical_role: Amos anchors justice, judgment, worship integrity, covenant accountability, and restoration within Minor Prophets, book 3 of 12 and connects the book to related people, places, events, and themes.
interpretive_disputes: How to read prophetic poetry, irony, and symbolic action

related_objects.notes: Justice is a defining concern in Amos.
Judgment addresses Israel and surrounding nations.
Amos sharply reframes expectation of the day of the Lord.
The book calls hearers away from injustice and false security.
The closing promise points toward restoration.
